excerpt: Traffic is the easiest website number to look at — and one of the least useful ones on its own. Here's what actually matters.
body:
Ask most remodeling business owners how their website is doing, and the answer usually comes back to one number: traffic. More visitors feels like progress. In practice, traffic on its own tells you almost nothing about whether your website is actually helping the business.

A website with 2,000 visitors a month and 3 leads is performing worse than a website with 400 visitors and 12 leads, even though the first one looks more impressive in a screenshot. The metrics worth watching are the ones that sit closer to revenue, not the ones that are easiest to glance at.

**Conversion rate, not just visitors**

The percentage of visitors who actually take an action — filling out a form, calling, booking a consultation — matters far more than raw traffic. A remodeler site converting at 3-5% of visitors into leads is generally healthy; below 1% usually points to a message or design problem, not a traffic problem, and no amount of additional traffic will fix that on its own.

**Where visitors actually come from**

Traffic from a Google search for "\[your city] kitchen remodeler" behaves very differently than traffic from a Facebook ad or a random blog link. Lumping all traffic together hides which sources are actually bringing in people ready to hire, versus people just browsing. Segmenting this — even just splitting "search," "social," "direct," and "referral" — usually reveals that one or two sources are doing most of the real work.

**Time on the portfolio or project pages**

For a high-end remodeler, the portfolio is often doing more selling than any single page of text. If visitors are landing on your homepage and leaving in under a minute, or never making it to your project photos at all, that's a strong signal the site isn't guiding people toward the content that actually builds trust and moves them toward reaching out.

**Form abandonment**

If your analytics can show you how many people start filling out a contact form but never submit it, that number is worth paying attention to. A high abandonment rate usually means the form is too long, asks for information too early, or feels like a commitment before the visitor is ready to make one.

**Lead source attribution, tied back to closed deals**

The most useful version of all this is connecting website data back to your CRM — which leads actually came from the website, and which of those actually closed. Without that connection, it's easy to overvalue a source that generates a lot of form fills but very few real customers, or undervalue a quieter source that consistently brings in serious buyers.

**Why this matters more than a redesign**

It's tempting to treat a stalling website as a design problem — new colors, a new layout, better photos. Sometimes that's the right call. But just as often, the site's design is fine and the real issue is invisible without looking at these numbers: the wrong traffic is arriving, or the right traffic is arriving and dropping off at a specific, fixable point. Tracking the right metrics is what tells you which situation you're actually in, instead of guessing and rebuilding a site that wasn't the problem in the first place.
